hints: Look at the shape and start and end pH values of the curve to decide if P and Q are strong or weak.
Notice the vertical jump happens at 10 cm3 of Q, even though you started with 20 cm3 of P at the same concentration.
Think about how many H+ ions per acid and OH- ions per base each option supplies, and which pair needs only half the volume to neutralise.
walkthrough:
**Identify the type of titration from pH**

The curve starts at pH about 0.5 and finishes at pH about 14. That very low start and very high finish is typical of a strong acid titrated with a strong base.

This rules out any weak acid like $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ (start pH 3 to 4) and any weak base like $\text{NH}_3$ (finish pH 9 to 11).

**Find the equivalence volume**

The steep vertical section is the end point. Here it is at about 10 cm3 of Q added.

$$V_Q \text{ at equivalence} \approx 10 \text{ cm}^3$$

**Use concentration and mole ratio**

P and Q have the same concentration, call it $c$. Moles in flask:
$$n(\text{P}) = c \times 20$$
Moles added at end point:
$$n(\text{Q}) = c \times 10$$
So 10 cm3 of Q must neutralise 20 cm3 of P. Q must supply twice as many $\text{OH}^-$ per mole as P supplies $\text{H}^+$ per mole.

**Match to the options**

$\text{HCl}$ supplies 1 $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ supplies 2 $\text{OH}^-$:
$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
One mole of base neutralises two moles of acid, so half the volume is needed. That gives exactly 10 cm3 to neutralise 20 cm3.

options.A: HCl with NaOH is strong acid with strong base, so the pH shape fits. However both are monobasic with 1 H+ and 1 OH-, so equal concentrations would need equal volumes, 20 cm3 of NaOH for 20 cm3 of HCl, not the observed 10 cm3.
options.B: H2SO4 is a strong diprotic acid, but NH3 is a weak base. The final pH with excess weak base would level off around 9 to 11, not near 14. Also 1 mole H2SO4 needs 2 moles NH3, so you would need about 40 cm3, not 10 cm3.
options.C: HCl is a strong monoprotic acid giving the very low starting pH, and Ba(OH)2 is a strong dibasic alkali giving the very high finishing pH. Since Ba(OH)2 gives 2 OH- per mole, only 10 cm3 at the same concentration is needed to neutralise 20 cm3 of HCl, matching the end point exactly.
options.D: CH3COOH is a weak acid, so 20 cm3 in the flask would start at pH about 3, not below 1. Although Sr(OH)2 is dibasic and would give a 10 cm3 end point for volume, the starting pH and the shape of the rise do not fit a weak acid with strong base.
